title: Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Thermal Properties of Matter

expression: Q = msΔT  (temperature change)  ;  Q = mL  (phase change, constant temperature)
explanation: Heat required to raise temperature (without a phase change) is Q = msΔT, where s is specific heat capacity — a material property describing how much heat is needed per unit mass per degree change. During a phase change (melting/boiling) at constant temperature, all supplied heat instead goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, given by Q = mL, where L is the latent heat (of fusion or vaporisation) — temperature stays constant throughout this phase.

workedExample.scenario: Heating 2 kg of water from 20°C to 100°C, then boiling it completely (Lv of water ≈ 2.26×10⁶ J/kg, s ≈ 4186 J/kg·K).
workedExample.result: Total Q ≈ 5.19 × 10⁶ J (boiling needs far more energy than heating!)

commonMistakes: Using the specific heat formula (Q=msΔT) during a phase change, where temperature isn't actually changing — the correct formula there is Q=mL, with no ΔT term at all.

Forgetting boiling/vaporisation typically requires much more energy than simply heating the same mass of liquid across its full temperature range — a genuinely large numerical gap worth sanity-checking.
genZNote: Boiling water takes way more energy than just heating it — the phase change is the real energy sink.
